summary: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) with widths up to 100 µm are tuned to their intrinsic performance limit using adjacent current-biased superconducting rails that redistribute current density across the wire width, achieving a ten orders-of-magnitude reduction in dark count rates and near-unity internal detection efficiency at 4 µm for 20 µm-wide detectors. This rail-based current redistribution suppresses edge vortex penetration, enabling operation limited only by vortex-antivortex pair unbinding in the bulk and overcoming the Pearl length ($\Lambda \approx 600$ µm) limitation on device width.
motivation: SNSPDs achieve high detection efficiency and low jitter but operate well below the depairing current $I_d$ due to current crowding at wire edges, which creates a fundamental barrier to scaling beyond the Pearl length and limits infrared sensitivity in wide devices.
method: The authors placed 4 µm-wide Nb rails (50 nm thick) adjacent to 3 nm-thick WSi SNSPD wires and varied the rail current $I_r$ to invert the current density profile $J(x)$, using London equation calculations and thermal transport measurements at 900 mK to characterize dark counts, photon detection, and timing jitter.
result: For a 50 µm-wide device, $I_r = I_r^* \approx 11.8$ mA increased the switching current ratio $I_{\mathrm{sw}}/I_d$ and extended the detection plateau at 1550 nm by 40%; for a 100 µm-wide device, more than 10 orders of magnitude dark count reduction and 44% plateau widening were achieved; near-unity internal detection efficiency was demonstrated at 4 µm for a 20 µm-wide detector (factor of 20 wider than prior state-of-the-art), with timing jitter improved by ~30%.
